strengths: This is an interesting and well written paper. To my knowledge, the learned graph for graph communication using transformers is a novel idea with clear applications to the real world. The architecture is simple/clear and the motivation for the necessity of this solution is motivated very well in Figure 1.
The CommFormer method significantly outperforms most of the baselines on most of the tasks (with the exception of some super hard SMAC tasks)
Performs ablative studies to demonstrate the importance of the sparsity claimed in the paper.
Adaptable to various actor-critic methods, not just PPO
Solid formalization of the communication graph problem
impressive experimental results on SMAC compared to SOTA methods
well written paper, a pleasure to read

This paper introduces a novel approach which models the communication architecture among agents as a learnable graph. The considered problem is formulated as the task of determining the communication graph while enabling the architecture parameters to update normally, thus necessitating a bi-level optimization process.
weaknesses: The problem formulation assumes communication can be created/destroyed between any arbitrary agents as long as a sparsity measure is met, which is a large assumption while claiming the CTDE paradigm.
The authors restrict communication of agent i to only agents j where j < i, assuming an implicit or explicit ordering of agents, which may impose additional nuances.
The authors do not compare to a recent graph-based MARL baseline called QGNN[1].

Fixed communication network after training; the lack of dynamic adjustments limits the applicability of the method in scenarios where communication needs change over time or the environment is non-stationary.
task 8m is not in figure 4 (as opposed to what the "Sparsity" paragraph would suggest in 4.3 Ablations).

The phrasing “Nevertheless, As task complexity and the number of participating agents increase, a higher level of sparsity becomes necessary to attain superior performance.” is confusing because it suggests that as complexity increases, fewer connections are needed, which is counterintuitive.

What if the communication graph determined by the approach is not physically feasible due to environmental constraints such as distance? A hybrid approach considering environment constraints may be needed.
The presented related work section is weak and relatively old; many recent SOTA graph-based multi-agent communication learning approaches are not mentioned or discussed.

Existing recent SOTA graph-based multi-agent communication learning approaches are not compared against; the selected benchmarks do not necessarily specialize in graph-based distributed communication, and the proposed approach should be evaluated against other graph-based methods.
All evaluations are performed in SMAC domains; it is unclear whether the approach generalizes to other domains and problem settings, which should be considered.
If the approach does not apply to other multi-agent problems and scenarios, this limitation should be mentioned and discussed.
The second contribution bullet-point mentions the use of attention units for allocating credit to received messages, which may already be done by TarMAC.
The limitations of the approach are never discussed.
It would be better to illustrate the differences of the paper compared to prior works that learn multi-agent cooperative behaviors based on learnable graphs.
The CTDE paradigm is not suited for the proposed communication-based MARL method; CTCE may be more appropriate, and CTCE-based MARL methods should be considered for comparison.
Using a fully connected communication graph as an upper bound is questionable; the 93.8% value for the FC column is not explained, making the upper bound determination unclear.
